Eurofins DiscoverX Sane Diego United States † Corresponding author ## Abstract Potent, selective and broadly characterized small molecule modulators of protein function (chemical probes) are powerful research reagents. The pharmaceutical industry has generated many high-quality chemical probes and several of these have been made available to academia. However, probe-associated data and control compounds, such as inactive structurally related molecules and their associated data, are generally not accessible. The lack of data and guidance makes it difficult for researchers to decide which chemical tools to choose. Several pharmaceutical companies (AbbVie, Bayer, Boehringer Ingelheim, Janssen, MSD, Pfizer, and Takeda) have therefore entered into a pre-competitive collaboration to make available a large number of innovative high-quality probes, including all probe-associated data, control compounds and recommendations on use (https://openscienceprobes.sgc-frankfurt.de/). Here we describe the chemical tools and target-related knowledge that have been made available, and encourage others to join the project. ## “Man must shape his tools lest they shape him” (Arthur Miller) The function of a protein can be explored in several different ways. Genetic approaches are used to suppress the expression of the respective gene/protein, for example using gene editing methods such as siRNA or shRNA or by CRISPR/Cas9 (Mali et al., 2013). However, in drug discovery, these methods have some deficiencies: they commonly remove or suppress the entire protein and thus cannot easily reveal the function of a specific druggable protein domain – although domain-based CRISPR is becoming a more widely used method; they are not reversible; their effects are not instantaneous; and they not only disrupt the protein, but also the protein interactome around the targeted protein. Selective small molecule modulators (‘chemical probes’), in contrast, can probe the particular function of a targeted domain and can, therefore, be used to study its role in biological processes and in human disease in a dose and time-dependent manner across a wide range of cell and animal models. These probes can also be modified to enhance the degradation of the protein(s) they bind to (Mali et al., 2013; Toure and Crews, 2016). Small molecules can be used in a broad panel of assay systems comprising primary cells, tissues and also in vivo models, and other systems not easily amenable even for state-of-the-art genetic target validation methods. Despite the fact that non-selective compounds cast a wide net and can be used to uncover interesting polypharmacologies, having a panel of selective probes that can be used in combination will facilitate data deconvolution and target identification. These properties, together with the possibility of further development of probes into drug candidates, make them among the most versatile tools to explore the relevance of a protein for therapeutic development. However, the necessary characterization data is often missing for chemical compounds, and inhibitors are announced as being ‘selective’ despite missing a comprehensive profile. Tool compounds, which are chemically unstable or not comprehensively characterized are therefore limited in their utility (Arrowsmith et al., 2015). Moreover, poorly characterized chemical modulators generate misleading results and litter the literature with contradicting data on a target’s function and its role in biology. This is also true for probes that are used improperly, e.g. at higher than appropriate concentration thus inhibiting other proteins in addition to the target or resulting in non-specific cellular toxicity. Unfortunately, reactive and non-specific inhibitors are widely used in the academic research community, often resulting in incorrect functional annotation (Baell and Walters, 2014). The ideal chemical probes need to be selective, active in cells and chemically stable. The recent discussion on best practice within the chemical biology community suggested a number of stringent quality criteria for chemical probes (Arrowsmith et al., 2015; Blagg and Workman, 2017; Edwards et al., 2009; Bunnage et al., 2013). Typical criteria as applied by the Structural Genomics Consortium (SGC) are shown in Figure 1, although these may vary slightly depending on the specific protein. ![Figure 1.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/34311/elife-34311-fig1-v2.jpg) **Figure 1.:** Shown here are target and compound related criteria applied by the Structural Genomics Consortium. A diverse set of chemical tool compounds is available to cell biologists. However, characterization data associated with these compounds are often either incomplete or buried in patents or supplemental data files of publications. Thus, scientists face a challenge to decide which tools to use for their research. Help is provided for example by the Chemical Probes Portal (Baell and Walters, 2014; Blagg and Workman, 2017), which was established in 2015 to provide a comprehensive overview of published and newly released tool compounds that are annotated with a simple star-rating system. All compounds submitted to the portal are reviewed by at least three members of an independent expert scientific advisory board. Only probes that receive three stars (‘Best available probe for this target, or a high-quality probe that is a useful orthogonal tool’) or four stars (‘Recommended as a probe for this target’) are recommended to be used. Of all the compounds submitted to the probe portal so far (about 400), 125 have achieved a rating of three stars or better, thereby showing that there is an urgent need for more high-quality tool compounds to foster reproducible research. ## “Excellence, then, is not an act, but a habit” (Will Durant [Durant, 1926]) Like drug discovery, probe development is a multi-disciplinary effort involving experts from several areas including protein chemistry, biochemistry, cell biology, pharmacology and medicinal chemistry (Dahlin and Walters, 2014; Garbaccio and Parmee, 2016). Once a target has been selected, the first step is the design of a project-specific screening cascade. The screening procedure needs to reflect target-related probe criteria as well as the desired compound properties. A typical screening cascade for a kinase probe discovery project is shown in Figure 2. The screening cascade consists of a primary assay – usually a biochemical activity assay – plus an assay with an orthogonal readout, e.g., a biophysical assay, a number of selectivity assays for the target and a cell-based assay to demonstrate on-target activity in the cellular environment. If possible, a crystallization system should be established to elucidate the binding modes of selected compounds enabling the rational design of better inhibitors. In silico analyses to exclude undesired events such as frequent hitters and pan-assay interference compounds (PAINs), and assays characterizing the physical and chemical properties of the identified hits (Hughes et al., 2011) complement the analysis (Baell and Walters, 2014). Medicinal chemistry optimization is then started for selected compound classes. For a typical project, multiple rounds of the Design – Make – Test – Analyze circle (Plowright et al., 2012) are needed before a suitable probe candidate is identified. Importantly, cross-correlating results from different assays within a compound class (e.g. tracking of cellular read-outs with biochemical potency and cellular target engagement data) provide a continuing consistency check if observed effects are truly a function of inhibiting the target of interest. Experience within the SGC shows that approximately 1–2 years and €2 million are needed to generate one chemical probe fulfilling these stringent criteria (Donner, 2014). This observation is in line with the experience of many medicinal chemists at pharmaceutical companies. ![Figure 2.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/34311/elife-34311-fig2-v2.jpg) **Figure 2.:** Medicinal chemistry optimization involving multiple iterative steps of compound design, synthesis and screening are necessary until probe criteria are fulfilled. As there may be similarities among binding sites on both related and unrelated proteins, unwanted binding to proteins other than the original target is regularly observed. This selectivity challenge can never be completely avoided, and thus the end users should be aware of unknown cross-reactivity challenges. A way to reduce the risk of non-specific effects is the use of a suitable control compound having a chemical structure closely related to that of the probe but lacking activity on the target. A wider profiling against a panel of pharmacologically active targets or proteomics analysis of the compound provides additional information about compound selectivity. Having access to multiple probes from structurally different chemical series further reduces the risk that unknown off-target activities give rise to incorrect conclusions about target functions. ## “Well begun is half done” (Aristotle) Many quality probe compounds are buried in the chemical vaults of the pharmaceutical industry, depriving the scientific community of useful tools and limiting the impact of the original research. In some cases, particular compounds, their properties and some structure–activity relationships (SAR) have been published (Nara et al., 2014; Siebeneicher et al., 2016; Takahashi et al., 2015; Wu-Wong et al., 1999). However, often only selected data are published and the proprietary compounds are not made available to the researchers except via restrictive contractual agreements, and this impedes their use and their impact. Indeed, in the nuclear hormone receptor field, we showed that any legal encumbrances to compound access reduced the subsequent use of the compound in the literature significantly (Isserlin, 2011). Thus, the open access/open science approach is the fastest route to reach the end users and thereby to have a positive effect on research. This evidence, as well as impact from the SGC epigenetics probes project, has convinced the SGC partner companies that the release of previously hidden compounds and data to the public will provide value to science and to the companies (Lee, 2015). To this end, seven pharmaceutical companies associated with the SGC have each agreed to donate 10 of these valuable compounds, stemming from their research pipelines, for a total of 70 high-quality small molecules, thus providing a major boost to the chemical biology toolbox. The compounds have been selected based on a variety of criteria, which are different for each participating company. These include profiling available for the compound, feasibility of generating a control compound, availability of physical compound, target class, intellectual property considerations, and other factors. This is an exciting development, but many of the compounds will require wider profiling to meet today’s more stringent quality criteria. As the primary focus of the pharmaceutical industry is not to generate chemical probes, but to develop new drugs, not all donated probes have been profiled to the same depth that is required of a high-quality chemical probe. Moreover, specificity for a particular target is not a requirement for an effective drug. Thus, although most of the pharma-donated probes have been extensively characterized, they often need to be better adapted for use as a single chemical tool (Figure 1). In particular, no bespoke control compounds have been generated as the progress of the probe compounds within the company is usually followed by extensive SAR across a series of analogues. Selection and characterization of the control compound is needed to complete a probe package. In addition, control compounds also have to be carefully characterized to weed out promiscuous compounds. The aim of our partnership is to provide this comprehensive characterization. We believe this to be a valuable contribution to the community. Once broadly characterized and accompanied by relevant control compounds, the initial set of 70 probes reflect a collective contribution of at least €140 million to the public domain (Figure 3). The targets of this first wave of probes are given in Table 1. Final numbers may slightly vary as some chemical probes are still in the approval process. In order to guarantee the quality of the compounds, the donated probe candidates and control compounds are subjected to a two-tier scientific review process: the first review takes place internally, including partners who have not been involved in the probe project, and the second review is performed by a panel of renowned scientists, who have agreed to act as independent reviewers. The first 30 proposals were presented to the internal review committee during a two-day meeting in June 2017 in Frankfurt am Main, Germany, where a process for their release to the public was also established. At this ‘historic’ meeting scientists from eight pharmaceutical companies scrutinized the quality of the probes proposed by the other partners and made constructive suggestions on improvement of the associated data packages (Figure 4A). In the initial set, most targets are uniquely addressed by only one chemical compound, but a maximum of two chemical probes for the same target will be accepted if they represent different chemotypes as judged by the review panels. The remaining probe sets will be provided during the course of 2018/2019. All approved probes are measured against the same quality criteria (Figure 1) and will be profiled in assay panels comprising of >500 assays, including broad panels of pharmacologically active targets such as GPCRs, kinases, ion channels and proteases to identify off-target activities (Table 2). Disease-specific phenotypic panels such as assays in primary tissues established by SGC partners will provide an initial characterization of their biological effects (Edwards et al., 2015). **Table 2.** Overview of data generated for all donated probes.These data will be made available through a publicly available database.

The proposed probes range from completely novel ‘best in class’, to probes that have been selected because they are provided as a complete set, with control compounds. Although some of the proposed compounds themselves are already commercially available, for most there is no widely characterized partner control compound (Figure 4B). ![Figure 4.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/34311/elife-34311-fig4-v2.jpg) The current probe proposals cover proteins from many different families such as GPCRs, kinases and proteases as well as other protein targets implicated in a variety of therapeutic areas ranging from oncology to inflammatory diseases and neurodegenerative disorders. An excellent example of a donated probe is the recently published p300/CBP histone acetyltransferase (HAT) inhibitor (A-485), which was shown to have efficacy in several cell models of malignancies (Lasko et al., 2017). This probe, including its control compound, has been approved by both internal as well as external reviewers and is now available to the scientific community. In contrast, other donated probes are not published or only mentioned in patents and therefore have not been accessible at all. Examples include a novel coagulation factor II thrombin receptor (F2R/PAR-1) inhibitor, which has potential for thrombosis management, and an inhibitor for focal adhesion kinase (FAK) and proline-rich tyrosine kinase 2 (PYK2), which has been in clinical trials for advanced non-haematologic malignancies, but for which profiling data have not yet been available. Even previously published probes are not always widely accessible. For example, the set includes a probe for the solute carrier NHE1, a target associated with ischemia/reperfusion-induced cell death, a peptidomimetic agonist for the KISS1 receptor, which plays a crucial role in cellular hormone function and puberty, and the inhibitor for a gamma secretase (GSI) protease, which may have potential in targeting Alzheimer’s disease. Using the infrastructure and established processes of past SGC probe projects, a non-bureaucratic and simple distribution process is implemented. This process involves distribution in bespoke probe libraries under a simple web-accessible Open Science Trust Agreement (http://www.thesgc.org/click-trust) as well as through trusted commercial vendors. To the best of our knowledge, our initiative is unique in enabling open access to well-validated probes including controls generated in the pharmaceutical industry for diverse target families. All supporting potency and selectivity data, as well as advice for the appropriate use of the compounds for cellular assays and – if applicable – in vivo assays, will be easily accessible via the public database (https://openscienceprobes.sgc-frankfurt.de/). The launch for the first version is planned for the beginning of 2018. The database supports the data needs of both biologists and chemists. The first version focusses on a search for the target proteins, probes, control compounds and recommendations on use. For the second version, additional features such as chemical substructure searches will be accessible. Full assay details will be provided and reagents used will be listed so that scientists using the probes are enabled to judge the quality of the data provided as well as to reproduce key data in their own lab. For example, it is important to know if a protein kinase has been screened in a binding or activity assay, and which ATP concentration has been used. Further, the protein construct used to perform certain assays is of significance. As both the probes and the negative controls will be characterized in more than 500 assays, we will generate more than 70,000 biological data sets within the next 1–2 years: a rich and easily accessible source for future analyses. By providing the data in a comprehensive way we hope to extend our understanding of this particular mechanism or protein in a way that leads to new therapeutic approaches. The new tool compounds and the corresponding data will help to improve the quality of research and will deepen our understanding of the target biology. However, comprehensive characterization, which ideally should be consistent to make data comparable and facilitate data mining, comes at a cost, and in many cases also requires resources for the (re-)synthesis of the chemical probe. The biggest problem is in the availability and characterization of the control compounds. Not all candidate probes will have a suitable similar analogue that does not inhibit/activate the target of interest. Funding will be necessary in order to fill such gaps, but financing such a project and the resources to synthesize and characterize compounds is no easy task. It does not usually fit into the remit of the major funding agencies and help is needed by relevant translational organizations and individual labs to support the project. Organizations like the Division of Pre-Clinical Innovation of the National Center for Advancing Translational Sciences (NCATS; https://ncats.nih.gov/) and the National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH) Psychoactive Drug Screening Program (https://pdspdb.unc.edu/pdspWeb/) housed at the laboratory of Dr Bryan Roth at UNC are generously supporting this crucial endeavour by synthesizing negative controls and conducting probe profiling experiments. The distribution of probes will occur via commercial vendors, but it is no trivial task to make the well-characterized control compounds available to the user. Due to reduced revenues from the control compounds, vendors are often reluctant to offer these important controls. Regrettably, researchers often perform experiments without the appropriate control compound due to cost reasons or because initial experiments have already been performed without the control. A trial kit, which we will offer, including both probe and control compound, and/or sets of pre-diluted compounds may aid researchers to perform properly controlled experiments from the start. It is up to the combined efforts of researchers, vendors, journal editors and referees to make use of the chemical probes in combination with their available control standard practice in biomedical research. ## “From a small seed a mighty trunk may grow” (Aeschylus) While in the past almost all aspects of pharmaceutical research and development (R&D) were seen as competitive, the thinking in the field has shifted remarkably over the last decade. More and more challenges in the R&D process are seen as precompetitive, resulting in public–private partnerships and multilateral, critical mass consortia jointly addressing overarching issues. Many pharmaceutical companies have initiated open innovation projects interacting with the academic community. A key success factor for these endeavours is the easy access to know-how and reagents without complicated contractual arrangements (Nilsson and Felding, 2015; Ehrismann and Patel, 2015). We hope that the project initiated here will entice other companies and academics to follow suit and join us in the quest to increase the availability of well-validated probes meeting stringent quality criteria for the scientific community and decide to make some of their assets openly available. Whilst ultimately, the success of the project will depend on the willingness and support of the scientific community, additional pharmaceutical companies and funding bodies to engage, we believe this is an exciting first step in uncovering and delivering high–quality chemical probes to unlock new biology and ultimately new high-quality targets for drug discovery.

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.34311.008](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.34311.008)

In the interests of transparency, eLife includes the editorial decision letter and accompanying author responses. A lightly edited version of the letter sent to the authors after peer review is shown, indicating the most substantive concerns; minor comments are not usually included.

Thank you for submitting your article "Donated Chemical Probes For Open Science" to eLife for consideration as a Feature Article. Your article has been reviewed by two peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by Emma Pewsey (as Associate Features Editor for eLife) and Peter Rodgers (the eLife Features Editor) as the Senior Editor. The reviewers have opted to remain anonymous.

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and I have drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

Summary:

The manuscript describes an important initiative that has the potential to significantly improve the quality of pharmacological agents available and further strengthen the use of chemical probes in many areas of biology. Importantly, probe-associated data generated internally, best use practices and inactive control compounds will also be shared. Thus, it will be of wide interest to the readers of eLife.

Essential revisions:

1) Please describe clearly how novel the donated probes are. No structures or names are provided for the probes listed in Table 1. Therefore, it is unclear in what way the current initiative is merely a repurposing/rebranding of other similar efforts or provides truly novel compounds. For example, the AbbVie P300/CBP inhibitor appears to be compound A-485, published in Nature 2017 and is currently available as an SGC probe and from several vendors. What constitutes the donation in that case, given that the compound is available, and data are already published? Similarly, are the Pfizer compounds those already currently available from Sigma for the same targets? Are the Boehringer Ingelheim compounds a subset of the ones made available in the opnMe initiative? Or are all these novel additional compounds?

2) High-quality probes already exist for several of the targets listed. Please include an analysis of the superiority of the new donated probes, indicating:

i) Targets for which there are currently no high-quality probes available;

ii) Targets for which the donated probe promises a significant (e.g. 10-fold) benefit in potency or selectivity;

iii) Cases in which the new donated probe has similar potency/selectivity as currently available probes but an entirely different chemotype;

iv) Cases where none of the above points apply (but there might still be a benefit in availability/control compounds/data annotation).

3) The purpose of the manuscript needs to be defined more clearly. Currently it is not clear whether the manuscript is primarily about defining chemical probes or about bringing awareness to the new resource.

4) Please provide more discussion about how the probes have been selected. It also needs to be made clear that the standards used for selection are not a definition of what a chemical probe is. Although having potent and selective inhibitor probes is ideal, non-selective chemical probes can also provide powerful information and should also be mentioned as good chemical probes.

claims.claim: Small molecules can be used in a broad panel of assay systems comprising primary cells, tissues and in vivo models.
claims.source: Small molecules can be used in a broad panel of assay systems comprising primary cells, tissues and also in vivo models, and other systems not easily amenable even for state-of-the-art genetic target validation methods.
claims.evidence: This describes the versatility of small molecules in various experimental systems.

claims.claim: Having a panel of selective probes that can be used in combination will facilitate data deconvolution and target identification.
claims.source: Despite the fact that non-selective compounds cast a wide net and can be used to uncover interesting polypharmacologies, having a panel of selective probes that can be used in combination will facilitate data deconvolution and target identification.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the utility of selective probes in research.

claims.claim: Chemical probes have the possibility of further development into drug candidates.
claims.source: These properties, together with the possibility of further development of probes into drug candidates, make them among the most versatile tools to explore the relevance of a protein for therapeutic development.
claims.evidence: This describes one of the advantages of chemical probes.

claims.claim: Necessary characterization data is often missing for chemical compounds.
claims.source: However, the necessary characterization data is often missing for chemical compounds, and inhibitors are announced as being 'selective' despite missing a comprehensive profile.
claims.evidence: This describes a problem in the field of chemical probes.

claims.claim: Tool compounds that are chemically unstable or not comprehensively characterized are limited in their utility.
claims.source: Tool compounds, which are chemically unstable or not comprehensively characterized are therefore limited in their utility (Arrowsmith et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Poorly characterized chemical modulators generate misleading results and litter the literature with contradicting data on a target's function.
claims.source: Moreover, poorly characterized chemical modulators generate misleading results and litter the literature with contradicting data on a target's function and its role in biology.
claims.evidence: This describes the negative consequences of using poorly characterized compounds.

claims.claim: Reactive and non-specific inhibitors are widely used in the academic research community, often resulting in incorrect functional annotation.
claims.source: Unfortunately, reactive and non-specific inhibitors are widely used in the academic research community, often resulting in incorrect functional annotation (Baell and Walters, 2014).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The ideal chemical probes need to be selective, active in cells and chemically stable.
claims.source: The ideal chemical probes need to be selective, active in cells and chemically stable.
claims.evidence: This defines the key criteria for ideal chemical probes.

claims.claim: The chemical biology community has suggested stringent quality criteria for chemical probes.
claims.source: The recent discussion on best practice within the chemical biology community suggested a number of stringent quality criteria for chemical probes (Arrowsmith et al., 2015; Blagg and Workman, 2017; Edwards et al., 2009; Bunnage et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: The Structural Genomics Consortium applies specific criteria for chemical probes as shown in Figure 1.
claims.source: Typical criteria as applied by the Structural Genomics Consortium (SGC) are shown in Figure 1, although these may vary slightly depending on the specific protein.
claims.evidence: This refers to specific criteria shown in a figure.

claims.claim: Characterization data associated with chemical tool compounds are often either incomplete or buried in patents or supplemental data files of publications.
claims.source: However, characterization data associated with these compounds are often either incomplete or buried in patents or supplemental data files of publications.
claims.evidence: This describes a problem with accessibility of compound characterization data.

claims.claim: The Chemical Probes Portal was established in 2015 to provide a comprehensive overview of published and newly released tool compounds.
claims.source: Help is provided for example by the Chemical Probes Portal (Baell and Walters, 2014; Blagg and Workman, 2017), which was established in 2015 to provide a comprehensive overview of published and newly released tool compounds that are annotated with a simple star-rating system.
claims.evidence: This provides factual information about when the portal was established and its purpose.

claims.claim: All compounds submitted to the Chemical Probes Portal are reviewed by at least three members of an independent expert scientific advisory board.
claims.source: All compounds submitted to the portal are reviewed by at least three members of an independent expert scientific advisory board.
claims.evidence: This describes the review process for the Chemical Probes Portal.

claims.claim: Only probes that receive three or four stars from the Chemical Probes Portal are recommended to be used.
claims.source: Only probes that receive three stars ('Best available probe for this target, or a high-quality probe that is a useful orthogonal tool') or four stars ('Recommended as a probe for this target') are recommended to be used.
claims.evidence: This describes the rating system and recommendations of the portal.

claims.claim: Of about 400 compounds submitted to the Chemical Probes Portal, 125 have achieved a rating of three stars or better.
claims.source: Of all the compounds submitted to the probe portal so far (about 400), 125 have achieved a rating of three stars or better, thereby showing that there is an urgent need for more high-quality tool compounds to foster reproducible research.
claims.evidence: This provides specific data about the portal's compound ratings.

claims.claim: There is an urgent need for more high-quality tool compounds to foster reproducible research.
claims.source: Of all the compounds submitted to the probe portal so far (about 400), 125 have achieved a rating of three stars or better, thereby showing that there is an urgent need for more high-quality tool compounds to foster reproducible research.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the low proportion of compounds meeting quality standards.

claims.claim: Probe development is a multi-disciplinary effort involving experts from several areas including protein chemistry, biochemistry, cell biology, pharmacology and medicinal chemistry.
claims.source: Like drug discovery, probe development is a multi-disciplinary effort involving experts from several areas including protein chemistry, biochemistry, cell biology, pharmacology and medicinal chemistry (Dahlin and Walters, 2014; Garbaccio and Parmee, 2016).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claims.claim: A typical screening cascade for a kinase probe discovery project is shown in Figure 2.
claims.source: A typical screening cascade for a kinase probe discovery project is shown in Figure 2.
claims.evidence: This refers to a figure showing the screening process.

claims.claim: The screening cascade consists of a primary assay, an assay with an orthogonal readout, selectivity assays, and a cell-based assay.
claims.source: The screening cascade consists of a primary assay – usually a biochemical activity assay – plus an assay with an orthogonal readout, e.g., a biophysical assay, a number of selectivity assays for the target and a cell-based assay to demonstrate on-target activity in the cellular environment.
claims.evidence: This describes the components of a typical screening cascade.

claims.claim: Multiple rounds of the Design – Make – Test – Analyze circle are needed before a suitable probe candidate is identified.
claims.source: For a typical project, multiple rounds of the Design – Make – Test – Analyze circle (Plowright et al., 2012) are needed before a suitable probe candidate is identified.
claims.evidence: This describes the iterative process of probe development with citation support.

claims.claim: Experience within the SGC shows that approximately 1–2 years and €2 million are needed to generate one chemical probe fulfilling stringent criteria.
claims.source: Experience within the SGC shows that approximately 1–2 years and €2 million are needed to generate one chemical probe fulfilling these stringent criteria (Donner, 2014).
claims.evidence: This provides specific data about the time and cost of probe development with citation support.

claims.claim: A suitable control compound should have a chemical structure closely related to that of the probe but lacking activity on the target.
claims.source: A way to reduce the risk of non-specific effects is the use of a suitable control compound having a chemical structure closely related to that of the probe but lacking activity on the target.
claims.evidence: This describes the characteristics of an appropriate control compound.

claims.claim: Having access to multiple probes from structurally different chemical series reduces the risk that unknown off-target activities give rise to incorrect conclusions about target functions.
claims.source: Having access to multiple probes from structurally different chemical series further reduces the risk that unknown off-target activities give rise to incorrect conclusions about target functions.
claims.evidence: This describes a strategy to improve research reliability.

claims.claim: Many quality probe compounds are buried in the chemical vaults of the pharmaceutical industry.
claims.source: Many quality probe compounds are buried in the chemical vaults of the pharmaceutical industry, depriving the scientific community of useful tools and limiting the impact of the original research.
claims.evidence: This describes the current state of probe accessibility.

claims.claim: In the nuclear hormone receptor field, any legal encumbrances to compound access reduced the subsequent use of the compound in the literature significantly.
claims.source: Indeed, in the nuclear hormone receptor field, we showed that any legal encumbrances to compound access reduced the subsequent use of the compound in the literature significantly (Isserlin, 2011).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claims.claim: The open access/open science approach is the fastest route to reach the end users and have a positive effect on research.
claims.source: Thus, the open access/open science approach is the fastest route to reach the end users and thereby to have a positive effect on research.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the previous evidence about legal encumbrances.

claims.claim: Seven pharmaceutical companies associated with the SGC have each agreed to donate 10 compounds, for a total of 70 high-quality small molecules.
claims.source: To this end, seven pharmaceutical companies associated with the SGC have each agreed to donate 10 of these valuable compounds, stemming from their research pipelines, for a total of 70 high-quality small molecules, thus providing a major boost to the chemical biology toolbox.
claims.evidence: This provides specific data about the number of compounds being donated.

claims.claim: Not all donated probes have been profiled to the same depth that is required of a high-quality chemical probe.
claims.source: As the primary focus of the pharmaceutical industry is not to generate chemical probes, but to develop new drugs, not all donated probes have been profiled to the same depth that is required of a high-quality chemical probe.
claims.evidence: This describes a limitation of the donated probes.

claims.claim: Specificity for a particular target is not a requirement for an effective drug.
claims.source: Moreover, specificity for a particular target is not a requirement for an effective drug.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about drug development principles.

claims.claim: Once broadly characterized and accompanied by relevant control compounds, the initial set of 70 probes reflect a collective contribution of at least €140 million to the public domain.
claims.source: Once broadly characterized and accompanied by relevant control compounds, the initial set of 70 probes reflect a collective contribution of at least €140 million to the public domain (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: This provides a specific valuation of the probe contribution.

claims.claim: The donated probes cover a broad array of targets from different protein families relevant for a number of disease indications.
claims.source: These donated probes cover a broad array of targets from different protein families relevant for a number of disease indications (see Table 1).
claims.evidence: This describes the diversity of the donated probes with reference to a table.

claims.claim: A-485 is a p300/CBP histone acetyltransferase (HAT) inhibitor that was shown to have efficacy in several cell models of malignancies.
claims.source: An excellent example of a donated probe is the recently published p300/CBP histone acetyltransferase (HAT) inhibitor (A-485), which was shown to have efficacy in several cell models of malignancies (Lasko et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published work.

claims.evidence: This describes one of the donated probes.

claims.evidence: This describes one of the donated probes and its clinical history.

claims.source: For example, the set includes a probe for the solute carrier NHE1, a target associated with ischemia/reperfusion-induced cell death
claims.evidence: This describes one of the donated probes and its target.

claims.evidence: This describes one of the donated probes and its target's function.

claims.source: and the inhibitor for a gamma secretase (GSI) protease, which may have potential in targeting Alzheimer's disease.
claims.evidence: This describes one of the donated probes and its potential application.

claims.claim: The donated probe candidates and control compounds are subjected to a two-tier scientific review process.
claims.source: In order to guarantee the quality of the compounds, the donated probe candidates and control compounds are subjected to a two-tier scientific review process: the first review takes place internally, including partners who have not been involved in the probe project, and the second review is performed by a panel of renowned scientists, who have agreed to act as independent reviewers.
claims.evidence: This describes the quality control process for the donated probes.

claims.claim: The first 30 proposals were presented to the internal review committee during a two-day meeting in June 2017 in Frankfurt am Main, Germany.
claims.source: The first 30 proposals were presented to the internal review committee during a two-day meeting in June 2017 in Frankfurt am Main, Germany, where a process for their release to the public was also established.
claims.evidence: This provides specific factual information about the review meeting.

claims.claim: A maximum of two chemical probes for the same target will be accepted if they represent different chemotypes.
claims.source: In the initial set, most targets are uniquely addressed by only one chemical compound, but a maximum of two chemical probes for the same target will be accepted if they represent different chemotypes as judged by the review panels.
claims.evidence: This describes a policy for probe selection.

claims.claim: All approved probes will be profiled in assay panels comprising of >500 assays.
claims.source: All approved probes are measured against the same quality criteria (Figure 1) and will be profiled in assay panels comprising of >500 assays, including broad panels of pharmacologically active targets such as GPCRs, kinases, ion channels and proteases to identify off-target activities (Table 2).
claims.evidence: This provides specific data about the profiling scope with reference to a table.

claims.claim: Disease-specific phenotypic panels will provide an initial characterization of the probes' biological effects.
claims.source: Disease-specific phenotypic panels such as assays in primary tissues established by SGC partners will provide an initial characterization of their biological effects (Edwards et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This describes additional characterization that will be performed with citation support.

claims.claim: Some of the proposed compounds are already commercially available, but most lack a widely characterized partner control compound.
claims.source: Although some of the proposed compounds themselves are already commercially available, for most there is no widely characterized partner control compound (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This describes the current state of control compound availability.

claims.claim: The current probe proposals cover proteins from many different families such as GPCRs, kinases and proteases.
claims.source: The current probe proposals cover proteins from many different families such as GPCRs, kinases and proteases as well as other protein targets implicated in a variety of therapeutic areas ranging from oncology to inflammatory diseases and neurodegenerative disorders.
claims.evidence: This describes the diversity of the probe targets.

claims.claim: Distribution of probes will occur via commercial vendors under a simple web-accessible Open Science Trust Agreement.
claims.source: This process involves distribution in bespoke probe libraries under a simple web-accessible Open Science Trust Agreement (http://www.thesgc.org/click-trust) as well as through trusted commercial vendors.
claims.evidence: This describes the distribution mechanism for the probes.

claims.claim: All supporting potency and selectivity data will be easily accessible via a public database at https://openscienceprobes.sgc-frankfurt.de/.
claims.source: All supporting potency and selectivity data, as well as advice for the appropriate use of the compounds for cellular assays and – if applicable – in vivo assays, will be easily accessible via the public database (https://openscienceprobes.sgc-frankfurt.de/).
claims.evidence: This describes how data will be made accessible.

claims.claim: The launch for the first version of the database is planned for the beginning of 2018.
claims.source: The launch for the first version is planned for the beginning of 2018.
claims.evidence: This provides a specific timeline for database launch.

claims.claim: The project will generate more than 70,000 biological data sets within the next 1–2 years.
claims.source: As both the probes and the negative controls will be characterized in more than 500 assays, we will generate more than 70,000 biological data sets within the next 1–2 years: a rich and easily accessible source for future analyses.
claims.evidence: This is calculated from the number of probes and assays.

claims.claim: NCATS and NIMH Psychoactive Drug Screening Program are supporting the project by synthesizing negative controls and conducting probe profiling experiments.
claims.source: Organizations like the Division of Pre-Clinical Innovation of the National Center for Advancing Translational Sciences (NCATS; https://ncats.nih.gov/) and the National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH) Psychoactive Drug Screening Program (https://pdspdb.unc.edu/pdspWeb/) housed at the laboratory of Dr Bryan Roth at UNC are generously supporting this crucial endeavour by synthesizing negative controls and conducting probe profiling experiments.
claims.evidence: This describes specific organizational support for the project.

claims.claim: Vendors are often reluctant to offer control compounds due to reduced revenues.

claims.evidence: This describes a challenge in making control compounds available.

claims.claim: Researchers often perform experiments without the appropriate control compound due to cost reasons or because initial experiments have already been performed without the control.
claims.source: Regrettably, researchers often perform experiments without the appropriate control compound due to cost reasons or because initial experiments have already been performed without the control.
claims.evidence: This describes a problem in current research practices.

claims.claim: The thinking in pharmaceutical R&D has shifted over the last decade, with more challenges seen as precompetitive.
claims.source: While in the past almost all aspects of pharmaceutical research and development (R&D) were seen as competitive, the thinking in the field has shifted remarkably over the last decade. More and more challenges in the R&D process are seen as precompetitive, resulting in public–private partnerships and multilateral, critical mass consortia jointly addressing overarching issues.
claims.evidence: This describes a trend in pharmaceutical research.

claims.claim: Many pharmaceutical companies have initiated open innovation projects interacting with the academic community.
claims.source: Many pharmaceutical companies have initiated open innovation projects interacting with the academic community.
claims.evidence: This describes a trend in pharmaceutical research.

claims.claim: Easy access to know-how and reagents without complicated contractual arrangements is a key success factor for open innovation endeavours.
claims.source: A key success factor for these endeavours is the easy access to know-how and reagents without complicated contractual arrangements (Nilsson and Felding, 2015; Ehrismann and Patel, 2015).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

results.result: Chemical probes are powerful research tools that offer advantages over genetic approaches for studying protein function. They can probe specific protein domains, work in a dose- and time-dependent manner across diverse experimental systems, can be modified for protein degradation, and have potential for drug development.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C10-C15 collectively establish the utility and advantages of chemical probes as research tools. These are well-established principles in chemical biology supported by general knowledge and the cited literature, making this a well-supported characterization of chemical probe capabilities.

results.result: Genetic approaches (siRNA, shRNA, CRISPR/Cas9) have limitations for drug discovery including: they remove entire proteins rather than specific domains, are not reversible, have non-instantaneous effects, and disrupt protein interactomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C9 describe well-established limitations of genetic approaches in the context of drug discovery. These are supported by citation (C5) and represent accepted knowledge in the field, though the manuscript acknowledges domain-based CRISPR is emerging (C6).

results.result: There is a significant problem with chemical probe quality in the research community: characterization data is often missing or inaccessible, poorly characterized compounds generate misleading results, and non-specific inhibitors are widely used leading to incorrect functional annotations.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C19 and C23 describe problems in the field that are supported by multiple citations (C17, C19) and represent a well-documented issue in chemical biology. This establishes the motivation for the current work.

results.result: The SGC has established stringent quality criteria for chemical probes including: biochemical potency <100 nM, cellular potency <1 μM, selectivity >30-fold within family, availability of inactive control compounds, tractable chemical matter without PAINs, appropriate solubility and stability, and biophysical proof of target engagement.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C22 and C68-C74 describe specific quality criteria supported by multiple citations (C21) and detailed in Figure 1. These represent established best practices in the field and are clearly documented in the manuscript.

results.result: The Chemical Probes Portal, established in 2015, provides quality ratings for chemical probes through independent expert review. Of ~400 compounds submitted, only 125 achieved 3+ star ratings, demonstrating an urgent need for more high-quality probes.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C28 and C67 provide specific data about the Chemical Probes Portal with citation support. The conclusion about urgent need (C28) is a reasonable inference from the low success rate (31% of compounds meeting quality standards).

results.result: Probe development is a multi-disciplinary, iterative process requiring multiple rounds of Design-Make-Test-Analyze cycles through screening cascades. SGC experience shows it takes approximately 1-2 years and €2 million to generate one high-quality chemical probe.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C33 describe the probe development process with citation support (C29, C32, C33). The cost and time estimates (C33) are based on SGC's documented experience, providing credible data for the resource requirements.

results.result: Control compounds with structures similar to probes but lacking target activity reduce the risk of non-specific effects, and having multiple probes from different chemical series further reduces risks from unknown off-target activities.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C35 describe best practices for reducing experimental artifacts. These are logical strategies supported by general principles in chemical biology, though they represent recommendations rather than experimental findings.

results.result: The pharmaceutical industry has generated many high-quality probes, but these are largely inaccessible along with associated data and controls. Evidence shows legal encumbrances significantly reduce compound usage in literature, making open access the fastest route to impact research.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C3 and C36-C38 establish the accessibility problem and rationale for open science. C37 provides specific evidence from the nuclear hormone receptor field with citation support, strengthening the argument for open access (C38).

results.result: Seven pharmaceutical companies have agreed to donate 70 high-quality compounds from their pipelines, representing a collective contribution of at least €140 million to the public domain. These probes cover diverse protein families and disease indications, though not all have been profiled to chemical probe standards since drug development doesn't require target specificity.
results.evaluation: Claims C4 and C39-C43 describe the core contribution of this initiative with specific, verifiable data. The €140 million valuation (C42) is calculated from the €2 million per probe estimate (C33), making it a reasonable inference. The acknowledgment of limitations (C40-C41) adds credibility.

results.result: Examples of donated probes include: A-485 (p300/CBP HAT inhibitor with demonstrated efficacy in malignancy models), a novel F2R/PAR-1 inhibitor for thrombosis, a FAK/PYK2 inhibitor from clinical trials, an NHE1 probe for ischemia/reperfusion, a KISS1 receptor agonist for hormone function, and a gamma secretase inhibitor with potential for Alzheimer's disease.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C49 provide specific examples of donated probes. C44 has citation support for demonstrated efficacy. The others describe probes with their targets and potential applications, though C49 appropriately uses cautious language ('may have potential') for the speculative Alzheimer's application.

results.result: A two-tier scientific review process (internal and independent external) ensures probe quality. The first 30 proposals were reviewed at a June 2017 meeting in Frankfurt where scientists from eight pharmaceutical companies evaluated each other's probes. A maximum of two probes per target are accepted if they represent different chemotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C52 and C75 describe the quality control process with specific details about the review meeting. This represents a concrete implementation of quality assurance, though the ultimate quality of approved probes depends on execution of the stated criteria.

results.result: All approved probes will undergo comprehensive profiling including: >500 assays covering kinases, GPCRs, ion channels, proteases, and epigenetic targets; target-specific assays and selectivity panels before release; phenotypic assays; and optional characterization including 3D structures, physicochemical parameters, and in vivo experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C54 and C112-C120 describe the planned characterization scope with specific numbers and assay types detailed in Table 2. This represents a concrete plan for comprehensive profiling, though evaluation is 'supported' for the plan rather than completed work.

results.result: Wave 1 includes approximately 9 GPCR and 4 kinase probes targeting diverse proteins across multiple families (GPCRs, kinases, hydrolases, ion channels, proteases, and other targets), with planned release in spring 2018. Most compounds lack widely characterized control compounds. Table 1 lists 27 specific probes with their targets, modes of action, and originating companies.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C56 and C82-C111 provide detailed information about Wave 1 probes supported by Table 1 and Figure 3. The specific probe counts (C82-C83) are visible in Figure 3, and all individual probes (C85-C111) are documented in Table 1, making this well-supported descriptive data.

results.result: Probes will be distributed via commercial vendors under an Open Science Trust Agreement, with all data accessible through a public database (openscienceprobes.sgc-frankfurt.de) launching in early 2018. The project will generate >70,000 biological datasets within 1-2 years from characterizing probes and controls in >500 assays.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C60 describe the distribution and data sharing plan with specific details. The 70,000 dataset calculation (C60) is straightforward: ~140 compounds (70 probes + 70 controls) × 500 assays = 70,000 datapoints, making this a well-supported projection.

results.result: NCATS and NIMH Psychoactive Drug Screening Program are supporting the project by synthesizing negative controls and conducting probe profiling experiments.
results.evaluation: Claim C61 describes specific organizational support with named institutions and their contributions. This represents a factual statement about project partnerships that can be verified.

results.result: Vendors are reluctant to offer control compounds due to reduced revenues, and researchers often perform experiments without appropriate controls due to cost or because initial experiments were already performed without controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C63 describe practical challenges in the field. While these are presented as general observations rather than systematic data, they represent plausible barriers to proper experimental design that motivate the project's emphasis on providing controls.

results.result: Pharmaceutical R&D thinking has shifted over the last decade toward viewing more challenges as precompetitive, resulting in public-private partnerships and open innovation projects. Easy access to reagents without complicated contractual arrangements is a key success factor.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C66 describe trends in pharmaceutical research with citation support (C66). These represent general observations about the field that provide context for the current initiative, supported by the cited literature.
